{{Short description|Mathematical theorem in stochastic processes}}
In the theory of [[stochastic process]]es in [[Discrete-time stochastic process|discrete time]], a part of the mathematical theory of [[probability theory|probability]], the '''Doob decomposition theorem''' gives a unique decomposition of every [[adapted process|adapted]] and [[integrable stochastic process|integrable]] stochastic process as the sum of a [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] and a [[predictable process]] (or "drift") starting at zero. The theorem was proved by and is named for [[Joseph L. Doob]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Doob|1953}}, see {{harv|Doob|1990|pp=296−298}}</ref>

The analogous theorem in the continuous-time case is the [[Doob–Meyer decomposition theorem]].

==Statement==
Let <math>(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})</math> be a [[probability space]], {{math|1=''I'' = {0, 1, 2, ..., ''N''}<nowiki/>}} with <math>N \in \N</math> or <math>I = \N_0</math> a finite or countably infinite index set, <math>(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in I}</math> a [[filtration (probability theory)|filtration]] of&nbsp;<math>\mathcal{F}</math>, and {{math|1=''X'' = (''X<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''∈''I''</sub>}} an adapted stochastic process with {{math|E[{{!}}''X<sub>n</sub>''{{!}}] < ∞}} for all {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I''}}. Then there exist a martingale {{math|1=''M'' = (''M<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''∈''I''</sub>}} and an integrable  predictable process {{math|1=''A'' = (''A<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''∈''I''</sub>}} starting with  {{math|1=''A''<sub>0</sub> = 0}} such that {{math|1=''X<sub>n</sub>'' = ''M<sub>n</sub>'' + ''A<sub>n</sub>''}} for every {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I''}}.
Here predictable means that {{math|''A''<sub>''n''</sub>}} is <math>\mathcal{F}_{n-1}</math>-[[measurable function|measurable]] for every {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I'' \ {0}<nowiki/>}}.
This decomposition is [[almost surely]] unique.<ref>{{harvtxt|Durrett|2010}}</ref><ref>{{harv|Föllmer|Schied|2011|loc=Proposition&nbsp;6.1}}</ref><ref>{{harv|Williams|1991|loc=Section&nbsp;12.11, part&nbsp;(a) of the Theorem}}</ref>

===Remark===
The theorem is valid word for word also for stochastic processes {{math|''X''}} taking values in the {{math|''d''}}-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\Reals^d</math> or the [[complex vector space]] <math>\Complex^d</math>. This follows from the one-dimensional version by considering the components individually.

==Proof==
=== Existence ===
Using [[conditional expectation]]s, define the processes {{math|''A''}} and {{math|''M''}}, for every {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I''}}, explicitly by
 
{{NumBlk|:|<math>A_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X_k\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{k-1}]-X_{k-1}\bigr)</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

and

{{NumBlk|:|<math>M_n=X_0+\sum_{k=1}^n\bigl(X_k-\mathbb{E}[X_k\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{k-1}]\bigr),</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

where the sums for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 0}} are [[empty sum|empty]] and defined as zero. Here {{math|''A''}} adds up the expected increments of {{math|''X''}}, and {{math|''M''}} adds up the surprises, i.e., the part of every {{math|''X<sub>k</sub>''}} that is not known one time step before.
Due to these definitions, {{math|''A''<sub>''n''+1</sub>}} (if {{math|''n'' + 1 ∈ ''I''}}) and {{math|''M<sub>n</sub>''}} are {{math|{{mathcal|F}}<sub>''n''</sub>}}-measurable because the process {{math|''X''}} is adapted, {{math|E[{{!}}''A<sub>n</sub>''{{!}}] < ∞}} and {{math|E[{{!}}''M<sub>n</sub>''{{!}}] < ∞}} because the process {{math|''X''}} is integrable, and the decomposition {{math|''X<sub>n</sub>'' {{=}} ''M<sub>n</sub>'' + ''A<sub>n</sub>''}} is valid for every {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I''}}. The martingale property

:<math>\mathbb{E}[M_n-M_{n-1}\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=0</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;[[Almost surely|a.s.]]

also follows from the above definition ({{EquationNote|2}}), for every {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I'' \ {0}}}.

=== Uniqueness ===
To prove uniqueness, let {{math|''X'' {{=}} ''M''{{'}} + ''A''{{'}}}} be an additional decomposition. Then the process {{math|''Y'' :{{=}}  ''M'' − ''M''{{'}} {{=}} ''A''{{'}} − ''A''}} is a martingale, implying that

:<math>\mathbb{E}[Y_n\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=Y_{n-1}</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a.s.,

and also predictable, implying that

:<math>\mathbb{E}[Y_n\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]= Y_n</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a.s.

for any {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I'' \ {0}}}. Since {{math|''Y''<sub>0</sub> {{=}} ''A''{{'}}<sub>0</sub> − ''A''<sub>0</sub> {{=}} 0}} by the convention about the starting point of the predictable processes, this implies iteratively that {{math|''Y<sub>n</sub>'' {{=}} 0}} almost surely for all {{math|''n'' ∈ ''I''}}, hence the decomposition is almost surely unique.

==Corollary==
A real-valued stochastic process {{math|''X''}} is a [[submartingale]] if and only if it has a Doob decomposition into a martingale {{math|''M''}} and an integrable predictable process {{math|''A''}} that is almost surely [[increasing]].<ref>{{harv|Williams|1991|loc=Section&nbsp;12.11, part&nbsp;(b) of the Theorem}}</ref> It is a [[supermartingale]], if and only if {{math|''A''}} is almost surely [[decreasing]].

===Proof===
If {{math|''X''}} is a submartingale, then

:<math>\mathbb{E}[X_k\,|\,\mathcal{F}_{k-1}]\ge X_{k-1}</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a.s.

for all {{math|''k'' ∈ ''I'' \ {0}}}, which is equivalent to saying that every term in definition ({{EquationNote|1}}) of {{math|''A''}} is almost surely positive, hence {{math|''A''}} is almost surely increasing. The equivalence for supermartingales is proved similarly.

==Example==
Let {{math|''X'' {{=}} (''X<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''∈<math>\mathbb{N}_0</math></sub>}} be a sequence in independent, integrable, real-valued random variables. They are adapted to the filtration generated by the sequence, i.e. {{math|{{mathcal|F}}<sub>''n''</sub> {{=}} ''σ''(''X''<sub>0</sub>, . . . , ''X<sub>n</sub>'')}}  for all <math>n \isin \mathbb{N}_0.</math> By ({{EquationNote|1}}) and ({{EquationNote|2}}), the Doob decomposition is given by

:<math>A_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[X_k]-X_{k-1}\bigr),\quad n\in\mathbb{N}_0,</math>

and

:<math>M_n=X_0+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl(X_k-\mathbb{E}[X_k]\bigr),\quad n\in\mathbb{N}_0.</math>

If the random variables of the original sequence&nbsp;{{math|''X''}} have mean zero, this simplifies to

:<math>A_n=-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}X_k</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<math>M_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}X_k,\quad n\in\mathbb{N}_0,</math>

hence both processes are (possibly time-inhomogeneous) [[random walk]]s. If the sequence {{math|''X'' {{=}} (''X<sub>n</sub>'')<sub>''n''∈<math>\mathbb{N}_0</math></sub>}} consists of symmetric random variables taking the values {{math|+1}} and&nbsp;{{math|−1}}, then {{math|''X''}}&nbsp;is bounded, but the martingale&nbsp;{{math|''M''}} and the predictable process&nbsp;{{math|''A''}} are unbounded [[simple random walk]]s (and not [[uniform integrability|uniformly integrable]]), and [[Doob's optional stopping theorem]] might not be applicable to the martingale&nbsp;{{math|''M''}} unless the stopping time has a finite expectation.

==Application==
In [[mathematical finance]], the Doob decomposition theorem can be used to determine the largest optimal exercise time of an [[American option]].<ref>{{harv|Lamberton|Lapeyre|2008|loc=Chapter&nbsp;2: Optimal stopping problem and American options}}</ref><ref>{{harv|Föllmer|Schied|2011|loc=Chapter&nbsp;6: American contingent claims}}</ref> Let {{math|''X'' {{=}} (''X''<sub>0</sub>, ''X''<sub>1</sub>, . . . , ''X<sub>N</sub>'')}} denote the non-negative, [[discounted cash flow|discounted]] payoffs of an American option in a {{math|''N''}}-period financial market model, adapted to a filtration {{math|
({{mathcal|F}}<sub>0</sub>, {{mathcal|F}}<sub>1</sub>, . . . , {{mathcal|F}}<sub>''N''</sub>)}}, and let <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>g denote an [[Equivalence (measure theory)|equivalent]] [[martingale measure]]. Let {{math|''U'' {{=}} (''U''<sub>0</sub>, ''U''<sub>1</sub>, . . . , ''U<sub>N</sub>'')}} denote the [[Snell envelope]] of&nbsp;{{math|''X''}} with respect to <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>. The Snell envelope is the smallest <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>-supermartingale dominating {{math|''X''}}<ref>{{harv|Föllmer|Schied|2011|loc=Proposition&nbsp;6.10}}</ref> and in a complete financial market it represents the minimal amount of capital necessary to hedge the American option up to maturity.<ref>{{harv|Föllmer|Schied|2011|loc=Theorem&nbsp;6.11}}</ref> Let {{math|''U'' {{=}} ''M'' + ''A''}} denote the Doob decomposition with respect to <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> of the Snell envelope&nbsp;{{math|''U''}} into a martingale {{math|''M'' {{=}} (''M''<sub>0</sub>, ''M''<sub>1</sub>, . . . , ''M<sub>N</sub>'')}} and a decreasing predictable process {{math|''A'' {{=}} (''A''<sub>0</sub>, ''A''<sub>1</sub>, . . . , ''A<sub>N</sub>'')}} with {{math|''A''<sub>0</sub> {{=}} 0}}. Then the largest [[stopping time]] to exercise the American option in an optimal way<ref>{{harv|Lamberton|Lapeyre|2008|loc=Proposition&nbsp;2.3.2}}</ref><ref>{{harv|Föllmer|Schied|2011|loc=Theorem&nbsp;6.21}}</ref> is

:<math>\tau_{\text{max}}:=\begin{cases}N&\text{if }A_N=0,\\\min\{n\in\{0,\dots,N-1\}\mid A_{n+1}<0\}&\text{if } A_N<0.\end{cases}</math>

Since {{math|''A''}} is predictable, the [[event (probability theory)|event]] {{math|{''τ''<sub>max</sub> {{=}} ''n''} {{=}} {''A<sub>n</sub>'' {{=}} 0, ''A''<sub>''n''+1</sub> < 0}}} is in&nbsp;{{math|{{mathcal|F}}<sub>''n''</sub>}} for every {{math|''n'' ∈ {0, 1, . . . , ''N'' − 1}}}, hence {{math|''τ''<sub>max</sub>}} is indeed a stopping time. It gives the last moment before the discounted value of the American option will drop in expectation; up to time&nbsp;{{math|''τ''<sub>max</sub>}} the discounted value process&nbsp;{{math|''U''}} is a martingale with respect to <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.

==Generalization==
The Doob decomposition theorem can be generalized from probability spaces to [[σ-finite measure|σ-finite measure spaces]].<ref>{{harv|Schilling|2005|loc=Problem&nbsp;23.11}}</ref>
